claim: There are three main theories on how human grasping movements are controlled.
source: There are three main theories on how human grasping movements are controlled.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, referencing the existence of multiple theoretical frameworks.

claim: Two theories state that grip aperture and the movement of the hand are controlled, differing in whether the wrist or the thumb of the hand is controlled.
source: Two of them state that grip aperture and the movement of the hand are controlled. They differ in whether the wrist or the thumb of the hand is controlled.
evidence: This describes existing theories in the literature, representing established knowledge about different theoretical positions.

claim: A third theory states that grasping is a combination of two goal-directed single-digit movements, each directed at a specific position on the object.
source: We have proposed a third theory, which states that grasping is a combination of two goal-directed single-digit movements, each directed at a specific position on the object.
evidence: This is the authors' own theoretical proposal, representing their position in the field.

claim: Adaptation acquired during single-digit movements transfers to the hand opening when subsequently grasping objects.
source: We show that adaptation acquired during single-digit movements transfers to the hand opening when subsequently grasping objects, leaving the movement of the hand unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: Adaptation acquired during single-digit movements leaves the movement of the hand unaffected during grasping.
source: We show that adaptation acquired during single-digit movements transfers to the hand opening when subsequently grasping objects, leaving the movement of the hand unaffected.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data showing no effect on grip position.

claim: The results provide strong evidence that grasping with the thumb and index finger is based on a combination of two goal-directed single-digit movements.
source: Our results provide strong evidence for our theory that grasping with the thumb and index finger is based on a combination of two goal-directed single-digit movements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing selective transfer of adaptation to grip aperture but not grip position.

claim: Jeannerod (1984) proposed that grasping consists of a transport component (movement of the wrist) that brings the hand to a location near the object and a grip component that ensures that the distance between the digits (grip aperture) changes in a manner that is appropriate for the size of the object.
source: Jeannerod (1984) proposed that grasping consists of a transport component (movement of the wrist) that brings the hand to a location near the object and a grip component that ensures that the distance between the digits (grip aperture) changes in a manner that is appropriate for the size of the object.
evidence: This is a description of a theory from the literature, supported by citation to Jeannerod (1984).

claim: Some researchers argue that the thumb is transported to a position on the object, with the index finger moving relative to the thumb to match grip aperture to the object's size.
source: Others argue that the thumb is transported to a position on the object, with the index finger moving relative to the thumb to match grip aperture to the object's size (Mon-Williams and McIntosh, 2000; Wing and Fraser, 1983).
evidence: This is a description of a theory from the literature, supported by citations to Mon-Williams and McIntosh (2000) and Wing and Fraser (1983).

claim: The trajectories of the tips of the digits when grasping is simply the combination of the trajectories of the same tips in goal-directed single-digit movements, whereby each tip is moved to a specific position on the object.
source: Finally, we have proposed that the trajectories of the tips of the digits when grasping is simply the combination of the trajectories of the same tips in goal-directed single-digit movements ('pointing'), whereby each tip is moved to a specific position on the object (Schot et al., 2011; Smeets and Brenner, 1999; Smeets and Brenner, 2001; Verheij et al., 2012; Voudouris et al., 2013).
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical position supported by multiple citations to their previous work.

claim: People can simultaneously adapt movements of the finger and thumb of one hand to opposite prismatic displacements.
source: We have previously shown that people can simultaneously adapt movements of the finger and thumb of one hand to opposite prismatic displacements (Schot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work, supported by citation to Schot et al. (2014).

claim: If grasping is controlled by planning the movement of the wrist and the opening and closing of the grip aperture, opposite adaptation acquired during single-digit movements would not be expected to transfer to grasping.
source: If, as Jeannerod (1984) suggested, grasping is controlled by planning the movement of the wrist and the opening and closing of the grip aperture, one would not expect opposite adaptation acquired during single-digit movements to transfer to grasping: the aftereffects of the opposite displacements of the wrist when adapting single-digit movements of the index finger and thumb will cancel each other during subsequent movements of both together when grasping, leaving the grip position unaltered.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from Jeannerod's theory about what should happen in the experimental paradigm.

claim: According to the wrist-and-aperture control theory, grip aperture will not be influenced by adapting pointing movements because it is irrelevant for single-digit movements.
source: The grip aperture will also not be influenced by adapting pointing movements because it is irrelevant for single-digit movements.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from the transport-grip theory about what should happen in the experimental paradigm.

claim: If the movement of the thumb is controlled rather than the wrist, adaptation of single-digit thumb movements should lead to an aftereffect in the transport of the thumb in the opposite direction to the visual displacement.
source: If it is not the wrist movement that is controlled, but the movement of the thumb, as proposed by Mon-Williams and McIntosh (2000) and Wing and Fraser (1983), adaptation of single-digit thumb movements should lead to an aftereffect in the transport of the thumb. This aftereffect will be in the opposite direction than the visual displacement of the thumb in the adaptation phase.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from the thumb-control theory about what should happen in the experimental paradigm.

claim: According to the thumb-control theory, the movement of the index finger relative to the thumb will remain unaffected by adaptation because grip aperture is irrelevant during a single-digit movement.
source: The movement of the index finger relative to the thumb will remain unaffected, again because grip aperture is irrelevant during a single-digit movement.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from the thumb-control theory about what should happen in the experimental paradigm.

claim: According to the thumb-control theory, grip position will show the aftereffect of adaptation of the thumb, without any alteration of grip aperture.
source: The prediction is thus that grip position will show the aftereffect adaptation of the thumb, without any alteration of grip aperture.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from the thumb-control theory about what should happen in the experimental paradigm.

claim: According to the two-digit control theory, adaptation during pointing movements should transfer to grip aperture but not to grip position.
source: Our own theory, based on the control of single-digit movements, predicts transfer of adaptation during pointing movements to the grip aperture, but not to the grip position, because when single-digit movements that are adapted in opposite directions are executed simultaneously, the aftereffects will cancel each other for the grip position, but will summate for grip aperture.
evidence: This is a logical prediction derived from the authors' theory about what should happen in the experimental paradigm.

claim: When single-digit movements are adapted in opposite directions (leftward for index finger, rightward for thumb), the predicted aftereffect is a rightward deviation of the index finger and a leftward deviation of the thumb, leading to a larger grip aperture.
source: So, if movements of the index finger are performed under leftward visual displacement and movements of the thumb are performed under rightward visual displacement during adaptation (thumb right), the predicted aftereffect is a rightward deviation of the index finger and a leftward deviation of the thumb, leading to a larger grip aperture.
evidence: This is a specific prediction derived from the authors' theory about the expected outcome of the experimental manipulation.

claim: When the visual displacements are reversed during adaptation, grip aperture should decrease.
source: When the visual displacements are reversed, grip aperture should decrease.
evidence: This is a specific prediction derived from the authors' theory about the expected outcome of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The adaptation of pointing with the tip of each of the two single digits was similar to the equivalent adaptation in a previous experiment (Schot et al., 2014).
source: The adaptation of pointing with the tip of each of the two single digits (central part of Figure 1A) was similar to the equivalent adaptation in our previous experiment (Schot et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of current experimental data with previously published results, supported by reference to Figure 1A.

claim: After removing the prisms, the digits' movements during grasping showed a clear aftereffect of the adaptation during pointing.
source: After removing the prisms, the digits' movements during grasping showed a clear aftereffect of the adaptation during pointing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: There was a clear aftereffect of adapting to prisms during single-digit pointing movements on the grip aperture in subsequent grasping trials.
source: Interpreted in terms of a transport- and grip-component, we found a clear aftereffect of adapting to prisms during single-digit pointing movements on the grip aperture on subsequent grasping trials.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Grip aperture increased after thumb right adaptation for both the small and large block.
source: In accordance with our theory that grasping can be regarded as simultaneous movements of the individual digits, grip aperture did increase after thumb right adaptation (and decrease after thumb left adaptation), both for the small and the large block (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Grip aperture decreased after thumb left adaptation for both the small and large block.
source: In accordance with our theory that grasping can be regarded as simultaneous movements of the individual digits, grip aperture did increase after thumb right adaptation (and decrease after thumb left adaptation), both for the small and the large block (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 1B.

claim: Grip position remained unaffected by the adaptation.
source: As the two digits were always adapted in opposite directions, we expected their average (which we use as a measure of grip position) to remain unaffected by the adaptation. Our results show that this is the case (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Statistical analysis showed a significant phase by session interaction for grip aperture (F(1,7)=7.3, p=0.03).
source: Statistical analysis of the effects of session, adaptation phase, and target block size on grip aperture showed a significant phase by session interaction (F(1,7)=7.3, p=0.03) indicating that grip aperture indeed changed differently after thumb left and thumb right adaptation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: The difference in grip aperture between thumb left and thumb right adaptation is 1.2 cm.
source: This difference is 1.2 cm.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: There was a significant effect of block size on grip aperture, with the target cuboid grasped with a 2.3 cm larger grip aperture than the target cube (F(1,7)=324.1, p<0.001).
source: Besides the phase by session interaction, there were also significant effects of block size (the target cuboid was grasped with a 2.3 cm larger grip aperture than the target cube; F(1,7)=324.1, p<0.001) and of session (F(1,7)=24.8, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis showing an expected effect of object size.

claim: There was a significant effect of session on grip aperture (F(1,7)=24.8, p=0.002).
source: Besides the phase by session interaction, there were also significant effects of block size (the target cuboid was grasped with a 2.3 cm larger grip aperture than the target cube; F(1,7)=324.1, p<0.001) and of session (F(1,7)=24.8, p=0.002).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis.

claim: Statistical analysis of grip position did not show any significant effects (all p>0.1).
source: Statistical analysis of the effects of session, adaptation phase, and target block size on the grip position did not show any significant effects (all p>0.1, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the data analysis, supported by Figure 1C.

claim: The difference in grip position corresponding to the non-significant tendency towards an adaptation phase by session interaction was only 0.1 cm, an order of magnitude smaller than the 1.2 cm found for grip aperture.
source: The difference corresponding to the non-significant tendency towards an adaptation phase by session interaction for grip position was only 0.1 cm, an order of magnitude smaller than the 1.2 cm that we found for grip aperture.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of measurements from the experimental data.

claim: During the first movement towards the small block after thumb left adaptation, one participant's digits came so close together that they touched each other.
source: During the first movement towards the small block after thumb left adaptation (solid red curve), this participant's digits came so close together that they touched each other, giving her haptic feedback that they should be further apart.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in the inset of Figure 1B.

claim: The measure of grip aperture gives an underestimation of the initial aftereffect because participants partly corrected their movement after receiving haptic feedback.
source: Thus, our measure of grip aperture gives an underestimation of the initial aftereffect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that digits touched and participants corrected their movements.

claim: Adaptation does not only transfer to grip formation, which primarily involves distal muscles, but also transfers to grip position, which primarily involves proximal muscles.
source: We have ascertained that adaptation does not only transfer to grip formation, which primarily involves distal muscles, but also transfers to grip position, which primarily involves proximal muscles. We did this by adapting both digits in the same direction (see Appendix 1 'Transfer to grip position').
evidence: This is a finding from an additional experiment described in Appendix 1.

claim: Transfer of prism adaptation has been shown to be absent or only partial when tested with a different movement speed.
source: Transfer of prism adaptation has been shown to be absent or only partial when tested with a different movement speed (Kitazawa et al., 1997), throwing style (Martin et al., 1996) or load (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transfer of prism adaptation has been shown to be absent or only partial when tested with a different throwing style.
source: Transfer of prism adaptation has been shown to be absent or only partial when tested with a different movement speed (Kitazawa et al., 1997), throwing style (Martin et al., 1996) or load (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transfer of prism adaptation has been shown to be absent or only partial when tested with a different load.
source: Transfer of prism adaptation has been shown to be absent or only partial when tested with a different movement speed (Kitazawa et al., 1997), throwing style (Martin et al., 1996) or load (Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Adaptation can be very specific to a particular movement.
source: This shows that adaptation can be very specific to a particular movement (van der Kooij et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a general conclusion from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: The fact that transfer from single-digit pointing to grip aperture in grasping was found is not trivial but suggests that grasping is indeed the combination of two single-digit movements.
source: The fact that we find transfer from single-digit pointing to the grip aperture in grasping is therefore not at all trivial but suggests that grasping is indeed the combination of two single-digit movements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings in the context of the literature on specificity of adaptation.

claim: Using the wrist as a proxy for grip position makes it necessary to add a third controlled variable because the position to which the wrist should be transported to grasp an object depends on the orientation of the hand and the size of the object.
source: We have previously noted that using the wrist as a proxy for grip position makes it necessary to add a third controlled variable because the position to which the wrist should be transported to grasp an object depends on the orientation of the hand and the size of the object (Smeets and Brenner, 1999).
evidence: This is a logical argument about the transport-grip theory, supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Evidence shows that adaptation is specific for the joints involved in the pointing movements.
source: In doing so, we ignore the evidence that adaptation is specific for the joints involved in the pointing movements (Krakauer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the literature, supported by citation.

claim: Participants mainly performed the pointing movements and their corrections from the elbow and shoulder.
source: Such evidence makes our findings even more surprising, because as can be seen in the example in Video 1, the participants mainly performed the pointing movements and their corrections from the elbow and shoulder, whereas changes in grip aperture must involve changing the angles of the digits relative to the hand.
evidence: This is an observation from the video data (Video 1).

claim: Changes in grip aperture must involve changing the angles of the digits relative to the hand.
source: Such evidence makes our findings even more surprising, because as can be seen in the example in Video 1, the participants mainly performed the pointing movements and their corrections from the elbow and shoulder, whereas changes in grip aperture must involve changing the angles of the digits relative to the hand.
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge about how grip aperture is controlled.

claim: The transfer found to grip aperture in grasping is not based on transfer of a joint-specific adaptation, but on a higher-level control of the trajectory of the digit in space.
source: This suggests that the transfer that we found to grip aperture in grasping is not based on transfer of a joint-specific adaptation, but on a higher-level control of the trajectory of the digit in space.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that different joints are used in pointing versus grasping, yet transfer still occurs.

claim: Finding transfer from transporting the separate digits in pointing to grip aperture in grasping contradicts the idea that grip aperture is controlled separately from transport of the hand or thumb.
source: Finding transfer from transporting the separate digits in pointing to grip aperture in grasping (Figure 1B) contradicts the idea that grip aperture is controlled separately from transport of the hand or thumb (see Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in relation to theoretical predictions.

claim: Finding that grip position was not systematically further to the left after thumb right adaptation contradicts the theory that the thumb determines the transport of the hand.
source: Finding that grip position was not systematically further to the left after thumb right adaptation (Figure 1C) contradicts the theory that the thumb determines the transport of the hand.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data in relation to theoretical predictions.

claim: Both the presence of an effect on grip aperture and the lack of effect on grip position are consistent with similar but independent adaptation of the movements of finger and thumb.
source: Both the presence of an effect on grip aperture and the lack of effect on grip position are consistent with similar but independent adaptation of the movements of finger and thumb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of experimental results.

claim: Finding that the grip aperture can increase as well as decrease depending on the direction of the adaptation shows that the effect is due to the adaptation itself, rather than uncertainty about the size of the object leading to a larger hand opening.
source: Finding that the grip aperture can increase as well as decrease depending on the direction of the adaptation shows that the effect is due to the adaptation itself, rather than for instance uncertainty about the size of the object leading to a larger hand opening.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bidirectional nature of the experimental effects.

claim: The observation that the digits sometimes touch each other during the grasping movement is consistent with independent adaptation of the movements of finger and thumb.
source: The observation that the digits sometimes touch each other during the grasping movement (as in the example in the inset of Figure 1B) is also consistent with independent adaptation of the movements of finger and thumb.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of digit contact during grasping movements.

claim: With independent control of the thumb and index finger, it is possible that people plan digit trajectories that cannot be executed simultaneously for anatomical reasons.
source: With independent control of the thumb and index finger, it is possible that people plan digit trajectories that cannot be executed simultaneously for anatomical reasons.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what could happen under independent control of the digits.

claim: Neither of the other theories can account for the digits touching each other during the grasping movement because if the aperture is controlled it is only expected to decrease until it matches the size of the object.
source: Neither of the other theories can account for the digits touching each other during the grasping movement because if the aperture is controlled it is only expected to decrease (after reaching maximal grip aperture) until it matches the size of the object.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the predictions of alternative theories.

claim: Grasping can be considered to be built up of the same movements as single-digit pointing.
source: Together, these results provide strong evidence that grasping can be considered to be built up of the same movements as single-digit pointing: grasping is the combination of two goal-directed single-digit movements (Smeets and Brenner, 1999).
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by citation to the authors' theory.

claim: Eight participants (25–29 years of age, two males) took part in the experiment.
source: Eight participants (25–29 years of age, two males) took part in the experiment after giving informed consent.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: Participants wore PLATO shutter glasses during the experiment.
source: They wore PLATO shutter glasses.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Movements of Infrared emitting diodes attached to the fingernails of the thumb and index finger were recorded at 250 Hz using an Optotrak 3020 system.
source: Movements of Infrared emitting diodes attached to the fingernails of the thumb and index finger were recorded at 250 Hz using an Optotrak 3020 system.
evidence: This is a description of the data collection method.

claim: The experiments consisted of three phases: pre- and post-adaptation phases which each consisted of 30 grasp trials, and an adaptation phase which consisted of 30 pointing trials with the thumb and 30 pointing trials with the index finger.
source: The experiments consisted of three phases: pre- and post-adaptation phases which each consisted of 30 grasp trials, and an adaptation phase which consisted of 30 pointing trials with the thumb and 30 pointing trials with the index finger.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Three objects were used: a starting cube (2.3 cm), a target cube (2.3 cm), and a target cuboid (2.3 × 2.3×4.6 cm).
source: Three objects were used: a starting cube (2.3 cm), a target cube (2.3 cm), and a target cuboid (2.3 × 2.3×4.6 cm).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: The target cuboid was included to force participants to use visual information to guide their grip aperture and to ensure that any observed adaptation effects are not specific to the object used in the adaptation phase.
source: It was included to force participants to use visual information to guide their grip aperture and to ensure that any observed adaptation effects are not specific to the object used in the adaptation phase.
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental design rationale.

claim: In the pre- and post-adaptation phases, participants viewed the target binocularly without prism glasses.
source: In the pre- and post- adaptation phases (i.e., on grasp trials), participants viewed the target binocularly without prism glasses.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: In the adaptation phase, participants viewed the target monocularly through 10 diopter prism glasses that were worn over the shutter glasses.
source: In the adaptation phase (i.e., on single-digit pointing trials), participants viewed the target monocularly through 10 diopter prism glasses that were worn over the shutter glasses.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The prism in front of the left eye shifted the image of the target about 5 cm to the right.
source: The prism in front of the left eye shifted the image of the target about 5 cm to the right.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The prism in front of the right eye shifted the image of the target about 5 cm to the left.
source: The prism in front of the right eye shifted the image of the target about 5 cm to the left.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The experiment consisted of two sessions that were performed on separate days with their order counterbalanced across participants.
source: The experiment consisted of two sessions that were performed on separate days with their order counterbalanced across participants.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: In one session, vision was displaced to the right when touching the cube with the index finger and to the left when touching the cube with the thumb (thumb left).
source: In one session, vision was displaced to the right when touching the cube with the index finger and to the left when touching the cube with the thumb (thumb left).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: In the other session, the displacements were reversed (thumb right).
source: In the other session, the displacements were reversed (thumb right).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The analysis was based on the marker position 1 cm before it crossed the far edge of the board to ensure the measure was not influenced by movement corrections based on visual feedback.
source: To make sure that we had a measure that is not influenced by movement corrections based on visual feedback, we based our analysis for both index finger and thumb on the marker position 1 cm before it crossed the far edge of the board.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method and its rationale.

claim: Grip aperture was calculated by taking the difference between the positions of the two digits.
source: We calculated the grip aperture by taking the difference between these positions for the two digits and the grip position by taking the average of these positions.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Grip position was calculated by taking the average of the positions of the two digits.
source: We calculated the grip aperture by taking the difference between these positions for the two digits and the grip position by taking the average of these positions.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Grip position was expressed relative to the target's position because three target positions were used.
source: As we used three target positions, grip position was expressed relative to the target's position.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method and its rationale.

claim: The adaptation effect was evaluated by comparing the median value in the pre-adaptation phase with the median value in the post-adaptation phase.
source: We evaluated the adaptation effect by comparing the median value in the pre-adaptation phase with the median value in the post-adaptation phase, both for grip aperture and grip position.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis method.

claim: Two repeated measures ANOVAs were performed with phase, session, and target block size as independent variables, one with grip position as the dependent variable and the other with grip aperture as the dependent variable.
source: To test the predictions that follow from the different theories on grasping (Table 1), we performed two repeated measures ANOVAs with phase (pre-adaptation, post-adaptation), session (thumb left, thumb right), and target block size (small, large) as independent variables. One ANOVA had grip position as the dependent variable and the other had grip aperture as the dependent variable.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis method.

claim: A significant phase by session interaction would indicate that the adaptation during the pointing trials transfers to the grasp trials.
source: A significant phase by session interaction would indicate that the adaptation during the pointing trials transfers to the grasp trials.
evidence: This is an explanation of how the statistical test relates to the research question.

claim: According to the theory that grip aperture and wrist position are controlled, opposite adaptation of the two digits during pointing would not be expected to influence grip position during grasping.
source: Table 1. Whether or not adapting the two digits to opposite prisms during pointing movements would be expected to influence grip position and grip aperture during subsequent grasping movements according to the three main theories about the control of grasping.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as a prediction from the transport-grip theory.

claim: According to the theory that grip aperture and wrist position are controlled, opposite adaptation of the two digits during pointing would not be expected to influence grip aperture during grasping.
source: Table 1. Whether or not adapting the two digits to opposite prisms during pointing movements would be expected to influence grip position and grip aperture during subsequent grasping movements according to the three main theories about the control of grasping.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as a prediction from the transport-grip theory.

claim: According to the theory that grip aperture and thumb position are controlled, opposite adaptation of the two digits during pointing would be expected to influence grip position during grasping.
source: Table 1. Whether or not adapting the two digits to opposite prisms during pointing movements would be expected to influence grip position and grip aperture during subsequent grasping movements according to the three main theories about the control of grasping.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as a prediction from the thumb-control theory.

claim: According to the theory that grip aperture and thumb position are controlled, opposite adaptation of the two digits during pointing would not be expected to influence grip aperture during grasping.
source: Table 1. Whether or not adapting the two digits to opposite prisms during pointing movements would be expected to influence grip position and grip aperture during subsequent grasping movements according to the three main theories about the control of grasping.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as a prediction from the thumb-control theory.

claim: According to the theory that finger position and thumb position are controlled, opposite adaptation of the two digits during pointing would not be expected to influence grip position during grasping.
source: Table 1. Whether or not adapting the two digits to opposite prisms during pointing movements would be expected to influence grip position and grip aperture during subsequent grasping movements according to the three main theories about the control of grasping.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as a prediction from the two-digit control theory.

claim: According to the theory that finger position and thumb position are controlled, opposite adaptation of the two digits during pointing would be expected to influence grip aperture during grasping.
source: Table 1. Whether or not adapting the two digits to opposite prisms during pointing movements would be expected to influence grip position and grip aperture during subsequent grasping movements according to the three main theories about the control of grasping.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 as a prediction from the two-digit control theory.
